content.title: About
content.content: Cheese and queso are dairy products made from coagulated milk. Cheese can be hard, semi‑hard or soft, while queso (the Mexican melted cheese) usually has a softer texture and a mild flavor. Both are rich in protein, calcium and fatty acids and are widely used in cuisines around the world.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheese has been known to humans for over 7,000 years; the earliest evidence comes from ancient Mesopotamia.
Queso means “cheese” in Spanish, but in culinary contexts it often refers to a processed meltable cheese used in tacos, nachos and sauces.
There are more than 1,800 varieties of cheese, differing by aging process, type of milk and region of production.
Traditional Mexican queso is often made from a blend of melted cheese, cream and spices, giving it a characteristic stretchy quality.
Cheese rinds can be repurposed to make broths and sauces, adding depth of flavor.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cheese and queso provide high levels of calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Milk protein in cheese supports muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheeses contain vitamin B12, riboflavin and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic properties
items.content: Some aged cheeses contain live cultures that can benefit gut microbiota.

items.title: Beneficial fatty acids
items.content: Certain cheeses contain conjugated linoleic acid (CLA), which may help maintain a healthy weight.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consuming cheese, especially soft and fresh varieties.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Many cheeses, particularly aged ones, are high in salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein can cause severe reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cheese and queso are energy‑dense foods; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Choking hazard with hard cheese
items.content: Hard cheese chunks can pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese can be enjoyed sliced, grated into salads, melted in hot dishes, casseroles and sauces. Queso is commonly used in Mexican cuisine: nachos, tacos, fajitas, and as a meltable sauce that creates a stretchy texture. To reduce fat intake, choose low‑fat cheese varieties or limit the amount of queso in recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cheese in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. Hard cheeses can last several months, soft cheeses up to a week. Keep queso in a sealed package to prevent drying. Discard any cheese that develops unwanted mold (except for intentionally rind‑aged varieties).
